subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Entropy is best described as a measure of:
options: The energy content of a system
The disorder or number of ways energy and particles can be arranged
questions.explain: Entropy measures dispersal of energy/matter, i.e. the number of accessible arrangements.

questions.q: Which change has the greatest positive entropy change?
options: Two gases reacting to form one gas
questions.explain: Sublimation solid→gas gives the largest increase in disorder, so ΔS is most positive.

questions.q: A difference between a theoretical (perfect ionic model) lattice enthalpy and the experimental Born–Haber value suggests:
options: Some covalent character in the bonding
questions.explain: A discrepancy indicates covalent character (polarisation), since the ionic model is imperfect.

questions.q: A reaction with ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0 is:
questions.explain: With ΔH positive and ΔS negative, ΔG is always positive, so it is never feasible.

questions.q: Using ΔHf, the enthalpy of a reaction is calculated as:
questions.explain: ΔHr = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants).

questions.q: The first electron affinity of a non-metal is usually:
questions.explain: Adding the first electron to a neutral gaseous atom releases energy, so it is exothermic.

questions.q: What does 'mean bond enthalpy' refer to?
options: The average energy to break a particular bond type, averaged over many compounds
The enthalpy to break one specific bond in one molecule
The energy released when a bond forms in the gas phase
The enthalpy of a bond at absolute zero
questions.explain: Mean bond enthalpy is averaged across a range of molecules containing that bond.

questions.q: In a calorimetry experiment, 50.0 g of water rises by 8.0 °C (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). What is q?
For an endothermic reaction with positive ΔS, the reaction becomes feasible when:
options: Temperature is low enough that TΔS < ΔH
Temperature is high enough that TΔS > ΔH
questions.explain: With ΔH>0 and ΔS>0, raising T makes TΔS exceed ΔH so ΔG becomes negative.

questions.q: Why do bond-enthalpy calculations give only approximate ΔH values?
options: Bond enthalpies are exact for each molecule
They assume the reaction is at 0 K
Mean bond enthalpies are averages and ignore the specific molecular environment
They only apply to ionic compounds
questions.explain: Mean values are averaged over many compounds, so they differ slightly from any specific molecule.

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state, such as O2(g)?
options: Equal to its enthalpy of atomisation
questions.explain: By definition an element in its standard state has ΔHf = 0.

questions.q: For the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), the sign of ΔS is:
options: Negative, gas moles decrease from 4 to 2
questions.explain: Moles of gas fall from 4 to 2, so disorder decreases and ΔS is negative.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy always endothermic?
options: Energy is released removing an electron
Energy must be supplied to overcome attraction between the nucleus and the electron removed
questions.explain: Removing an electron from a gaseous atom requires energy to overcome nuclear attraction.

questions.q: In a Born–Haber cycle, the lattice enthalpy of formation refers to:
options: Breaking 1 mol of ionic lattice into gaseous ions
Forming 1 mol of ionic lattice from gaseous ions (exothermic)
questions.explain: Lattice enthalpy of formation is the exothermic formation of the lattice from gaseous ions.

questions.q: When solid NaCl dissolves, the enthalpy of solution equals:
options: Lattice dissociation enthalpy + sum of hydration enthalpies
questions.explain: ΔHsol = ΔH(lattice dissociation, +) + ΣΔH(hydration, −).

questions.q: Why is the second electron affinity of oxygen endothermic?
options: Energy is needed to add an electron to an already negative O⁻ ion against repulsion
Oxygen has a full outer shell
The nucleus attracts the electron strongly
questions.explain: Adding an electron to a negative O⁻ requires overcoming repulsion, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: The standard enthalpy of neutralisation is approximately constant for strong acids and strong alkalis at about −57 kJ mol⁻¹. Why?
options: Water has a fixed heat capacity
All acids release the same number of protons
The reaction is always H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
questions.explain: For strong acid/strong base, the underlying reaction is always H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

questions.q: A reaction is feasible (spontaneous) when:
questions.explain: A reaction is thermodynamically feasible when ΔG is negative.

questions.q: The enthalpy of atomisation of an element is the enthalpy change to form:
options: 1 mol of gaseous atoms from the element
questions.explain: Atomisation forms 1 mol of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state.

questions.q: For H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, using E(H–H)=436, E(Cl–Cl)=242, E(H–Cl)=431 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH is:
The standard enthalpy of combustion is measured when 1 mol of a substance:
options: Reacts completely with oxygen under standard conditions
questions.explain: ΔHc is the enthalpy change burning 1 mol completely in oxygen under standard conditions.

questions.q: Burning 0.0050 mol of a fuel raises 100 g of water by 20.0 °C (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). What is the enthalpy of combustion?
Given ΔHf[CO2] = −394 and ΔHf[H2O] = −286 kJ mol⁻¹, and ΔHc[CH4] = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, calculate ΔHf[CH4] (combustion gives CO2 + 2H2O).
For an exothermic reaction, which is true of the reaction profile?
options: Products are lower in energy than reactants and ΔH is negative
Products are higher in energy than reactants
questions.explain: Exothermic reactions release energy so products lie below reactants and ΔH < 0.

questions.q: Which process is always exothermic?
questions.explain: Forming bonds releases energy, so bond making is exothermic.

questions.q: Why are experimental enthalpies of combustion usually less exothermic than data-book values?
options: Heat loss to surroundings and incomplete combustion
Water has too large a heat capacity
The fuel is impure and burns hotter
questions.explain: Heat is lost to the surroundings and combustion is often incomplete, lowering the measured value.

questions.q: A reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0 is:
questions.explain: With ΔH negative and ΔS positive, ΔG is negative at all temperatures.

questions.q: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is:
options: Independent of the route taken, depending only on initial and final states
questions.explain: Hess's law: ΔH depends only on initial and final states, not the pathway.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +50 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The temperature at which it becomes feasible is:
questions.explain: At ΔG=0, T = ΔH/ΔS = 50000/100 = 500 K (above this it is feasible).

questions.q: Which factors increase the magnitude (more exothermic) of a lattice enthalpy?
options: Larger ionic radii and smaller charges
Smaller ionic radii and larger ionic charges
questions.explain: Smaller, more highly charged ions give greater electrostatic attraction and a more exothermic lattice enthalpy.
